ambiguities.issue: The paper uses inconsistent correction-count terminology for p = 2. [PDF pp. 11-12, anchors: Figure 2 setup and final p = 2 paragraph]

contract_plain_english: For p = 2, the corrected implicit midpoint method first solves one implicit stage with F^epsilon, then applies one explicit correction with F, and finally updates with F at the corrected stage. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-c)] Its coefficient cancellations remove the previous local O(epsilon Delta t^2) term, and, if the perturbed method is stable, the paper expects global Error = O(Delta t^2) + O(epsilon Delta t^2). [PDF p. 11, anchor: cancellation paragraph and displayed error] Figure 2 empirically shows slope two for this corrected variant, including the half- and single-precision cases, while the paper is inconsistent about whether to call p = 2 one correction or two correction steps. [PDF pp. 11-12, anchors: Figure 2 setup and final p = 2 paragraph]

source_evidence.anchor: equation (3.7), uncorrected mixed-precision implicit midpoint rule

source_evidence.anchor: corrected implicit midpoint method (4.1), Butcher arrays, and displayed global error
source_evidence.observation: The method performs one low-precision implicit stage followed by a high-precision explicit correction; its printed coefficients make b^epsilon(c-tilde) and (b-tilde)c^epsilon zero, and the paper states the stable global error O(Delta t^2) + O(epsilon Delta t^2).

source_evidence.anchor: Figure 2 setup and interpretation immediately below equation (4.1)
source_evidence.observation: The numerical study identifies p = 1 as no correction and p = 2 as one correction, using zero-, half-, and single-precision perturbation levels.

source_evidence.anchor: final paragraph interpreting the p = 2 corrected method
source_evidence.observation: The p = 2 curves have slope two; the half- and single-precision curves coincide with the complete double-precision curve in this experiment, while the epsilon = O(1) curve has a larger error but slope two.

statement.algorithm_linkage: This contract is specifically for the p = 2 corrected mixed-precision implicit midpoint construction (4.1): one approximate implicit midpoint stage, one full-precision explicit correction stage, and a full-precision update. [PDF p. 11, anchors: Eq. (4.1a-c) and Figure 2 setup paragraph]
binders: The selected corrected method binds the current value u^n, step size Delta t, full-precision operator F, approximate operator F^epsilon, initial stage y_[0]^(1), corrected stage y_[1]^(1), and update u^(n+1). [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-c)]
For the selected p = 2 variant, p-1 = 1 in the update, so the update evaluates F at y_[1]^(1); page 11 calls this one correction. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1c) and Figure 2 setup paragraph]

The state dimension is not specified in the theorem-like claim; the numerical demonstration specializes to the two-component van der Pol system. [PDF p. 11, anchor: global-error display and numerical-results paragraph; PDF p. 3, anchor: Eq. (2.5)]
conclusions: For p = 2, method (4.1) is y_[0]^(1) = u^n + (Delta t/2)F^epsilon(y_[0]^(1)), y_[1]^(1) = u^n + (Delta t/2)F(y_[0]^(1)), and u^(n+1) = u^n + Delta t F(y_[1]^(1)). [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-c), specialized using p = 2 from the Figure 2 setup paragraph]
The paper gives A = [[0,0],[1/2,0]], c = [0,1/2], b = [0,1], A^epsilon = [[1/2,0],[0,0]], c^epsilon = [1/2,0], and b^epsilon = [0,0]. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Butcher arrays below Eq. (4.1)]
It also gives A-tilde = [[1/2,0],[1/2,0]], c-tilde = [1/2,1/2], and b-tilde = [0,1]. [PDF p. 11, anchor: combined Butcher arrays below Eq. (4.1)]

Because b^epsilon(c-tilde) = 0 and (b-tilde)c^epsilon = 0, the paper says the O(epsilon Delta t^2) term in the one-step expansion is eliminated. [PDF p. 11, anchor: coefficient identities below the arrays]

If stable under the low-precision perturbation, the corrected method has expected global error Error = O(Delta t^2) + O(epsilon Delta t^2). [PDF p. 11, anchor: displayed global error below the coefficient identities]

In Figure 2, the p = 2 corrected method exhibits slope sigma = 2 for half and single precision and follows the complete double-precision error curve; for epsilon = O(1), it still has slope two but a larger error. [PDF p. 12, anchor: final paragraph on the p = 2 method]
constants_and_indexing: The midpoint coefficient is exactly 1/2 in both the low-precision implicit stage and the explicit correction. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-b)]
Correction-stage subscripts begin at 0; for p = 2 the available stages are [0] and [1], and the update uses subscript p-1 = 1. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-c) and p = 2 labeling]

The hidden constants in O(Delta t^2) and O(epsilon Delta t^2), including their dependence on epsilon, solution derivatives, and final time, are not specified. [PDF p. 11, anchor: displayed global error]
definitions_and_conventions: The first stage y_[0]^(1) is an implicit low-precision solve because its right-hand side contains F^epsilon evaluated at y_[0]^(1). [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a)]
The stage y_[1]^(1) is an explicit high-precision correction because it evaluates F at the already computed y_[0]^(1). [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1b) and preceding sentence]
Page 11 identifies p = 1 with no correction and p = 2 with one correction. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Figure 2 setup paragraph]

The experimental labels are epsilon = O(1) for zero precision, epsilon = O(10^-4) for half precision, and epsilon = O(10^-8) for single precision. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Figure 2 caption and Numerical Results paragraph]
error_notions: The displayed Error is a global error envelope with a second-order scheme contribution and a second-order epsilon-scaled perturbation contribution. [PDF p. 11, anchor: displayed error form below Eq. (4.1)]

The eliminated O(epsilon Delta t^2) quantity is a term in the one-step expansion, whereas O(epsilon Delta t^2) in the final displayed envelope is a global contribution; these are different uses of the same monomial order at different stages of the discussion. [PDF pp. 10-11, anchors: correction motivation and coefficient-cancellation paragraph]

Figure 2 reports numerical error versus Delta t, but the surrounding text does not define the exact subtraction or normalization used to calculate that plotted error. [PDF pp. 11-12, anchor: Figure 2 and its interpretation]
exceptional_values: No conditions concerning overflow, underflow, subnormals, NaN, infinity, implicit-solver failure, or nonexistence/nonuniqueness of y_[0]^(1) are stated with method (4.1). [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1) and its error discussion]
higher_order_terms: The paper presents only the global envelope O(Delta t^2) + O(epsilon Delta t^2); it does not display the remaining local perturbation coefficient or an explicit higher-order remainder for method (4.1). [PDF p. 11, anchor: cancellation paragraph and displayed global error]
The two O-terms have the same Delta t exponent, so the stated p = 2 envelope does not contain a lower-order-in-Delta-t perturbation term. [PDF p. 11, anchor: displayed global error]
hypotheses: The global error envelope is explicitly conditional on method (4.1) being stable under a low-precision perturbation. [PDF p. 11, anchor: sentence immediately before the displayed error form]
F^epsilon inherits the framework assumption that it approximates F to O(epsilon). [PDF p. 4, anchor: paragraph below Eq. (3.1); PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a)]

The p = 2 conclusion uses the displayed coefficient cancellations b^epsilon(c-tilde) = 0 and (b-tilde)c^epsilon = 0, which eliminate the local O(epsilon Delta t^2) term present in the uncorrected expansion. [PDF p. 11, anchor: coefficient arrays and paragraph below them; PDF p. 10, anchor: correction motivation]
The empirical statements are specific to the van der Pol test with parameter a = 1, initial data y1(0) = 2 and y2(0) = 0, and final time T_f = 1.0. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Numerical Results paragraph]
implicit_context: Method (4.1) corrects the mixed-precision implicit midpoint method (3.7), whose uncorrected stable global error is O(Delta t^2) + O(epsilon Delta t). [PDF p. 10, anchor: opening of Section 4.1.1; PDF p. 8, anchor: Eq. (3.7)]

The result is an asymptotic global-error statement inherited from the additive Runge-Kutta framework, not an exact equality or an unconditional stability result. [PDF p. 11, anchor: conditional displayed error form; PDF p. 2, anchor: standing stability qualification]

The empirical coincidence with the double-precision curve is a statement about Figure 2, not a theorem that the computed values are exactly equal. [PDF p. 12, anchor: final paragraph interpreting Figure 2]
norms: No norm or componentwise/relative-error convention is stated for the theoretical Error or the Figure 2 error axis. [PDF pp. 11-12, anchors: displayed global error and Figure 2 interpretation]
numerical_model: F^epsilon is used only in the implicit stage, while both the correction and final update use F. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-c)]

The paper describes the experiment through nominal epsilon levels O(1), O(10^-4), and O(10^-8), but does not impose an IEEE rounding mode or an operation-level floating-point error model on method (4.1). [PDF p. 11, anchor: Figure 2 caption and Numerical Results paragraph]

The framework allows low precision to represent an inaccurate implicit solve rather than requiring that every arithmetic operation be performed in a lower hardware format. [PDF p. 3, anchor: implicit-solver tolerance and Eq. (2.3); PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a)]

undebatable_constraints: The p = 2 method must retain the low-precision implicit stage, the full-precision explicit correction, and the full-precision update in exactly that order. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-c)]
The coefficient 1/2 and stage indices [0] and [1] are part of the selected algorithm, not adjustable constants. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Eq. (4.1a-b)]
The claimed theoretical envelope is global Error = O(Delta t^2) + O(epsilon Delta t^2) and is conditional on stability under the perturbation. [PDF p. 11, anchor: conditional displayed error form]

The p = 2 numerical slope-two behavior must be identified as experimental evidence from Figure 2 rather than promoted to an unconditional theorem. [PDF p. 12, anchor: final paragraph interpreting Figure 2]
The selected corrected variant is p = 2, which page 11 identifies as one correction after the initial approximate implicit stage. [PDF p. 11, anchor: Figure 2 setup paragraph]
